title: What Young People Owe the Future: A Climate Scientist's Perspective

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: Good morning. I want to start with something I find myself saying more and more: the science of climate change is settled. That is not a controversial statement among scientists. What remains deeply contested is not the science but the politics, the economics, and the ethics — and those are exactly the domains where every citizen, not just every scientist, has both a right and a responsibility to engage.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: I have spent twenty years studying glaciers and ice sheets. In that time, I have watched ice that took thousands of years to accumulate disappear in decades. I have taken measurements year after year, watching the numbers tell a story that I wished, for a long time, were not true. The data are not abstract to me. They have names — specific glaciers, specific places, specific communities that will be affected when the ice is gone.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: But I do not stand here to frighten you. Fear without agency is despair, and despair is not useful. What I want to talk about is agency — the power that individuals, communities, and nations have to shape the future. Because the future is genuinely not yet determined. The choices we make in the next decade will shape the climate of the next century. Not completely — some changes are now locked in. But the difference between acting now and acting in ten years is measured in millions of people's lives and the survival of entire ecosystems.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: The technological tools we need for a large part of the transition already exist. Solar and wind power are now the cheapest sources of electricity in history. Electric vehicles are becoming mainstream. Heat pumps can replace gas boilers with lower running costs. Battery storage is improving rapidly. The question is no longer primarily "can we do it?" The question is "will we choose to?" And that is a question answered not in laboratories but in parliaments, boardrooms, and ballot boxes.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: I want to speak specifically to young people. I know there is something called climate anxiety — a pervasive sense of dread about the future that many young people describe. I understand it. It is a rational response to irrational inaction. But I want to offer a counter-perspective: every generation has faced an enormous, seemingly intractable problem. The scale of this one is extraordinary. And yet the young people I meet who are working on climate solutions — designing clean energy systems, campaigning for policy change, building sustainable agriculture — are some of the most energised and purposeful people I have encountered in my career.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: What you owe the future is not perfection. You are not required to live without carbon emissions — that is not currently possible. What you owe is effort, informed by evidence, guided by values, and expressed in both personal choices and political engagement. It is to take this problem seriously, to stay informed, and to refuse to accept a future that can still be changed.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurlanova
dialogue.text: I have been asked many times: "Are you hopeful?" My honest answer is: I am neither hopeful nor despairing. I am determined. Determination is better than hope because it does not depend on circumstances. It depends on will. And the will to act is still, even now, available to every person in this room.
